  T18 in the plan:
  - A campaign list showing "Scheduled for …" and linking each resend to its
    parent campaign.

  Right now DashboardView.vue and CampaignsView.vue are empty placeholders.

  What the backend already gives T18:
  - GET /api/campaigns returns the newest 200 campaigns. It has no filters and
    no message counts for campaigns that have started sending.
  - GET /api/campaigns/{id}/events streams live status updates. Each channel
    reports:
    - the audience size;
    - message counts by status;
    - retries and rate-limit (429) responses;
    - skip reasons and the top failure reasons;
    - uncertain deliveries, how many could be resent, and any active resend.
  - The stream sends end once the campaign is finished (D36). The page must then
    close the connection and reload the campaign after a resend.
  - POST …/cancel and POST …/resend {channel} are ready.

  Gaps between the design and the backend: the README flagged these to settle in
  T18.
  1. Recipient details (design board 5): no API lists recipients or their
     delivery attempts.
  2. 429 count: the design shows "in the last 5 minutes"; the stream only has
     totals.
  3. "Uncertain": a flag on a message, not a status, so it would be shown as its
     own count.
  4. Resend: the design approves a shorter SMS in one dialog. In the backend a
     resend is a draft that goes through the T17 content and review screens
     (D31).

  There's also one I found while reviewing:

  5. Dashboard page (board B): no endpoint adds up numbers across campaigns. A
     summary of all campaigns would need a new endpoint or one live connection
     per campaign.

  Small items left from the T17 review:
  - Some screen-reader announcements are wrong or missing.
  - Wrong wording in the "changed elsewhere" race after Stop.
  - Logging out within 1.5 s of typing loses that last edit.
  - Some flake risk in the browser tests.

  CASE.md only asks to "show live delivery status on the dashboard", so most of

⏺ The full T18 plan is written in docs/plans/2026-10-23-t18-plan.md and includes
  Recipient Details. I haven't implemented or committed anything.

  Documented so far:
  - D45 in DECISIONS.md: Recipient Details is part of T18, with the requirements
    you set (paginated, filterable, statuses, failure reasons, attempt history,
    privacy, TR/EN).
  - The design details below are listed under Open Questions until you approve
    them. They become D46 onwards after approval.

  What T18 delivers, as your boards show it:
  - Dashboard (B): status cards and "Your campaigns".
  - Campaigns list (C): status filters, search by brief, and the actions for
    each status.
  - After approval:
    - A scheduled campaign shows its send time and can be cancelled.
    - A sending or finished campaign shows live delivery (board 4).
  - Recipient Details (board 5): a side panel opened from any status row.
  - Resend.

  Decisions the plan needs you to approve:

  - A. Status groups. In the backend "uncertain" is a flag on a message, but
    your design shows it as its own group. I propose:
    - Uncertain: failed, skipped or cancelled, where an attempt may still have
      gone through.
    - Sent: sent, even if an earlier attempt timed out.
    - Pending: pending, and messages being sent right now.
    - Retrying: waiting for another attempt.
    - Failed, Skipped, Cancelled: everything else in those statuses.

    The groups always add up to the audience, and the live screen and Recipient
    Details use the same definition.
  - B. Reasons as codes, not provider text. For example "Provider rejected",
    "Retries exhausted", "Over the limit (165 / 160)", "Consent revoked" and
    "Timeout". The UI translates each code. Raw provider error text is never
    sent to the browser.
  - C. Changes to the live status stream. It gains the groups, the reason codes
    and a "429s in the last 5 minutes" count, as in your design. It drops the
    raw error strings. The frontend doesn't use these fields yet, so nothing
    breaks.
  - D. Recipient API: GET 
    /api/campaigns/{id}/recipients?group=&channel=&q=&page=
    - 50 rows per page, newest attempt first.
    - Each row includes its attempt history.
    - Privacy:
      - Contacts are masked on the server: +90 555 ••• •• 17 and
        ays•••@example.com.
      - Search covers names only, never phone or email, so the API can't be used
        to check whether someone is a customer.
      - No message text or other customer fields are returned.
      - Responses are not cached (no-store).
    - Tests confirm that a full phone number or email never appears in any
      response.
    - Paging is by page number. While a campaign is still sending, rows can move
      between pages, so the panel shows the time its counts were taken, as your
      design does.
  - E. Resend uses the T17 screens. Board 6 edits and approves the shorter SMS
    on one page. In the backend a resend is a draft with its own approval (D31).
    So:
    a. A dialog shows who gets the resend and who doesn't.
    b. It then opens the follow-up campaign's content step, with the original
       SMS available to view.
    c. The resend is approved on the existing review step.
  - F. Campaign list search and filters run in the browser. They work on the
    newest 200 campaigns the list endpoint already returns. This limit goes in
    the README.
  - G. No "N SMS can be resent" hint on dashboard rows. It would need a count
    for every campaign. The resend offer is on each campaign's page instead.

  Steps: 8, each with its own tests and commit:
  1. Status groups and reasons in the stream.
  2. The recipients API.
  3. Frontend view logic with Vitest tests.
  4. Dashboard and campaign list.
  5. Scheduled and live campaign page.
  6. Recipient Details panel.
  7. Resend.
  8. TR/EN text, browser tests and docs.

  make test, make lint and make e2e all run before the task is reported done.

  Not in T18: the small leftovers from the T17 review, and any export or search
  by phone or email.

  Open risk: decision A changes what "uncertain" means in the status stream.
  It's an API change, although the frontend doesn't use the field yet. I haven't
  yet checked that the over-limit length (165 / 160) can be computed for each
  row with the existing content helpers; that happens in step 2.

  Do you approve the plan, including A–G, or do you want changes first?

⏺ Step 1 is done and committed locally in two commits; nothing is pushed. The
  full Go suite, the frontend tests and type check, and lint all pass.

  What changed: the live status stream (/events) now reports, for each channel:
  - groups: the seven display groups from the plan (sent, uncertain, failed,
    skipped, cancelled, retrying, pending). They always add up to the audience.
  - reasons: reason codes for each group, such as provider_rejected,
    retries_exhausted, character_limit_exceeded, no_consent and timeout.
    Provider error text is no longer sent.
  - rate_limited_recent: 429 responses in the last 5 minutes, next to the
    existing total.

  The old raw failure-reason strings and the separate uncertain count are
  removed. The frontend didn't use either yet.

  Two new reason codes appeared while I was writing the SQL:
  - requeued: a message waiting for a retry that was handed back without being
    sent, which happens on a worker shutdown.
  - no_response_recorded: an uncertain delivery with no attempt on record,
    because a worker died mid-attempt.

  One change from the approved plan: I removed the uncertain count rather than
  redefining it. It would have repeated groups.uncertain exactly. D46 now says
  so; tell me if you'd rather keep the field.

  Tests: a new test covers every group:
  - an uncertain flag on a sent message still counts as Sent;
  - uncertain on failed, skipped and cancelled messages counts as Uncertain;
  - each reason code, including the two new ones;
  - a 429 from 10 minutes ago appears only in the total;
  - the groups add up to the audience.

  Commits:
  - 5dfa57a: the T18 plan, and D45–D49 recorded as accepted.
  - 8cad08f: step 1, with the README's description of the stream updated.

  Next is step 2, the recipients API. Shall I go ahead?

  I haven't measured how fast the snapshot is on a full 6,000-message campaign.
  It only looks up attempts for failed, skipped, cancelled and retrying
  messages, which keeps it small. The session exports 05 and 06 are still not
  committed and need a check for personal data first.

⏺ Step 2 is done and committed locally as 236761d; nothing is pushed. The full
  Go suite and lint pass.

  The new endpoint: GET /api/campaigns/{id}/recipients?group=&channel=&q=&page=
  - Filters: group is required and is one of the seven display groups. channel
    is optional. q searches first and last name only, folding Turkish letters
    and case, so AYSE finds Ayşe and isil finds Işıl. % and _ are matched
    literally.
  - Paging: 50 rows per page, page 1 to 1000, newest attempt first.
  - What a row contains:
    - name and masked contact (+90 555 ••• •• 17, ays•••@example.com)
    - channel and reason code
    - for a character-limit skip, the length over the limit (e.g. 165 / 160),
      worked out on the server
    - the next attempt time when retrying
    - the attempt history: time, outcome and HTTP status
  - Also returned: the time the data was read (as_of), counts per group and
    channel for the tabs, reason counts for the group, and the total matching
    the filter.
  - Privacy:
    - A full phone number or email never leaves the server.
    - No city, message text or provider error text is returned.
    - Responses are marked Cache-Control: no-store, and sign-in is required.
    - An email address keeps at most 3 characters of its local part and never
      more than half of it, so a@example.com becomes •••@example.com.

  Tests:
  - Each group, reason code and the over-limit length.
  - Name search, including Turkish letters, wildcards and searching across first
    and last name together.
  - Paging across 121 rows and sorting by last attempt.
  - Masking: every page's raw response is scanned for full contacts, the city
    and error text, plus unit tests for unusual formats.
  - Bad input returns 422, an unknown campaign 404, a draft returns empty, and a
    signed-out request 401.

  The tests passed the first time they ran. So I removed the email masking and
  the wildcard escaping on purpose, and the tests failed for both. Then I
  restored the code.

  Docs: the README's API table has the new endpoint.

  Two things you should know:
  - Changed data shows up in a row's detail. The length over the limit uses the
    customer's current name. If the name changed after the skip, the number can
    differ from what was sent, or be missing.
  - Not measured for speed. I didn't time it on a full 3,000-recipient campaign.
    Sorting does one small lookup per message in the chosen group.

  Next is step 3: the frontend logic (counts, campaign list and recipient query
  state) with Vitest tests. Shall I continue?

⏺ I benchmarked the recipient API with 3,000 customers and made the large page
  about 5× faster. Step 3, the frontend logic, is also done. Both are committed
  locally; nothing is pushed. The full Go suite, lint, all 296 frontend tests

  Performance (c1e7798)

  The benchmark uses the real seed of 3,000 customers and a campaign that
  reached all of them on both channels: 6,000 messages with a typical mix of
  outcomes. It also adds 9 older campaigns, then 29, to see whether speed
  changes as campaigns pile up. It prints the query plan for every statement the
  API runs.

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────┬───────────────┐
  │            Request (ms)             │      Before       │     After     │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ Sent, first page (5,100 rows)       │               103 │            19 │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ Sent, last page                     │               110 │            17 │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ Name search                         │                58 │            19 │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ Failed / skipped / pending          │             12–22 │         10–14 │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ Live status snapshot, runs every    │ 24 → 45 with more │ 19–22 at both │
  │ second per open screen              │           history │         sizes │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────┴───────────────┘

  What the plans showed, and the fixes:
  1. Wasted lookups. The recipient API looked up each message's last attempt for
     every message in the group, about 30,000 lookups per request, even for
     sent messages, which have no reason to show. Now:
     - the totals don't do these lookups at all;
     - the reason counts run only for groups that have reasons;
     - the page picks its 50 rows first, and only those 50 get the lookups.
  2. The live status slowed down as campaigns piled up. It read every attempt
     ever recorded to count retries and 429s, so it got slower with every
     campaign sent. Now it reads only this campaign's attempts and skips sent
     messages that took one attempt, about 85% of them. That query went from 18
     ms to 5 ms and stays the same as history grows.

  Not done, with the reason: sorting by last attempt is now most of the
  remaining time, about 15 ms per request. Removing it needs a new stored column
  and a change in the sending worker. That isn't worth it for a panel opened by
  hand.

  The method, the results, the plan findings and the upgrade paths are in
  docs/performance.md, linked from the README.

  Step 3: frontend logic (eab184f)

  This is pure TypeScript with Vitest tests, no screens yet:
  - Delivery status (web/src/delivery/status.ts):
    - Phase: scheduled, sending, completed, cancelled, or cancelled before
      sending.
    - Totals: total, sent, not sent, uncertain, in progress, and the share
      finished.
    - Estimate vs actual per channel.
    - Bar segments.
    - When resend is offered: waiting while sending, available with the count,
      an active resend, or nobody left.
  - Campaign list (web/src/campaign/list.ts):
    - counts per status and the status filter;
    - search in the brief, ignoring case and Turkish letters;
    - the dashboard order: sending, then drafts, then scheduled by send time,
      then the newest finished;
    - the actions for each status.
  - Recipient filters (web/src/delivery/recipients.ts):
    - the panel's filters are kept in the address, so Back closes it and a link
      reopens it, and bad values fall back to defaults;
    - the API address, counts per tab in your design's order, and the "Showing
      X–Y of N" paging.

  One finding while writing the estimate comparison: the estimate stored at
  approval counts people, while the live numbers count messages per channel. So
  the screens compare channel by channel, and the totals compare messages, never
  people with messages.

  Next is step 4, the Dashboard and Campaigns pages. The benchmark ran in Docker
  on a laptop, so the absolute numbers will differ elsewhere; the before/after
  ratios and the history check are what count. The two session exports (05, 06)
  still need a check for personal data before they're committed.

⏺ Step 7, the resend flow, is built and committed locally in two commits
  (1521f54 and e940dcc); nothing is pushed. Every suite passes: Go, 330 Vitest
  tests, the type check, the TR/EN text scan, lint, and the full browser suite
  (all 9 files).

  Where the resend is offered: each channel on the delivery page shows a "Resend
  a shorter SMS" box with one of four states:
  - While sending: "Available when sending finishes."
  - Finished, with recipients to reach: "152 skipped for the character limit ·
    est. 152 can be resent" and a Resend to ~152… button.
  - Resend already exists: a link to it, and no second offer.
  - Nobody left to reach: an explanation, for example that they revoked consent.

  The recipient panel's Skipped tab offers the same thing. The panel closes and
  the dialog opens.

  The dialog (board 6's two panels):
  - Who gets the resend: skipped for the character limit, minus those no longer
    eligible, gives the eligible count, marked as an estimate that is checked
    again when the resend starts.
  - Not included: consent revoked, uncertain (they may already have it), and
    failed (a shorter message wouldn't help). For a two-channel campaign it also
    says the other channel isn't included.
  - Create the resend draft opens the follow-up's content step. A "Show original
    SMS" disclosure there shows the original message, and approval happens on
    the normal review step (D48).
  - If someone else created the resend meanwhile, the dialog shows the server's
    reason and the page updates to link to the existing resend.

  Tests:
  - Unit test for the dialog's numbers. I wrote it and the small function
    together, so I didn't see it fail first.
  - Browser checks: they failed before the screens existed and pass now. They
    cover:
    - the offer count against the API, the dialog's numbers, and opening it from
      the panel;
    - the full flow: create, check the draft's link and channel, show the
      original, write a shorter SMS, approve, wait until sent;
    - the resend's audience is exactly the eligible skipped recipients, and none
      were skipped again for length;
    - links in both directions, and no second offer;
    - the conflict case: the resend is created through the API while the dialog
      is open.

  I loosened one of my own checks. It required every resend message to end as
  Sent, but the mock provider fails some messages on purpose, so it would have
  been flaky. It now checks the audience, which is what D31 guarantees.

  I compared the dialog's screenshot with board 6, and it matches its two
  panels.

  Docs: the README's open design questions are now listed as settled, each
  pointing to its decision (D46–D49).

› Message from general-purpose
  ## Frontend core review, PR #6 (origin/milestone-f-frontend @ bc417f6, web/
  only)

  This review was read-only. I traced every finding through the code paths
  involved. I ran no tests, builds or npm commands.

  ### Critical
  None found.

  ### High
  **1. web/src/views/NewCampaignView.vue:24-44 + :84 — clicking "Interpret"
  again while it is busy creates a second campaign.**
  - **Defect:** `interpret()` never checks `busy`, and the button uses
  `aria-disabled`, which still lets clicks through. Login and reinterpret do
  have this guard.
  - **Scenario:** the AI interpretation takes a few seconds. The marketer clicks
  again, or double-clicks. Two `POST /api/campaigns` calls run, giving two
  drafts and two AI calls. They are routed to whichever create returns last, and
  the other draft is left orphaned in the list.
  - **Fix:** add `if (busy.value) return` at the top of `interpret()`.

  ### Medium
  **2. web/src/layouts/AppLayout.vue:24-27 with ContentView.vue:139 — signing
  out silently drops unsaved message text.**
  - **Defect:** `signOut` calls `logout()` first, which clears the session in
  `finally`, and only then navigates. ContentView's leave guard sees
  `session.value === null` and leaves without saving or asking.
  - **Scenario:** the marketer types into the SMS body and opens the account
  menu within the 1.5 s typing pause, or with the email incomplete. They click
  Sign out and the edit is lost with no prompt.
  - **Fix:** navigate away first so the guard can save or ask, and only log out
  if that navigation succeeds. For example: `if (await router.push({ name:
  'dashboard' })) return;` then call `logout()` and `replace('/login')`.
  vue-router returns a failure object when a guard blocks the navigation.

  **3. web/src/views/ReviewView.vue (whole file) — the approval page never shows
  the D40 "content may not match the new brief" warning.**
  - **Defect:** only CampaignView and ContentView read `contentWasStale`.
  - **Scenario:** the marketer re-interprets the brief on step 1, then uses
  StepBar (StepBar.vue:16, which links straight to Review) to jump to Review.
  They approve messages written for the old brief, and the approval page itself
  gives no warning. D40 says the warning must come "before approval".
  - **Fix:** add `const stale = contentWasStale(id)` and the same
  `alert-warning` banner to ReviewView. Optionally make it an approval blocker.

  ### Low
  **4. web/src/views/ContentView.vue:190-215 + :267 — the header says "Saved"
  after a generation that was stopped or failed.**
  - **Defect:** for the `stopped` and `failed` outcomes the queued op returns
  `fresh`, so the saver state becomes `'saved'`.
  - **Scenario:** the marketer clicks Stop, D34 says nothing is saved, yet the
  header reads "Saved".
  - **Fix:** throw a sentinel, or have the header ignore the state when
  `result.outcome !== 'done'`.

  **5. web/src/campaign/client.ts:73-77 and ContentView.vue:206-209 — plausible
  stale version after the connection drops mid-stream.**
  - **Defect:** a network `TypeError` from `reader.read()` is rethrown, so the
  page skips the `campaigns.get` refetch.
  - **Scenario:** if the server had already committed `saveContent`
  (content.go:83, a narrow window), the page keeps the old version. The next
  autosave gets a 409, and the "changed elsewhere, reload" banner appears for
  the marketer's own generation.
  - **What would confirm it:** dropping the connection right after the server
  commits.
  - **Fix:** treat any stream error like an abort: refetch, then decide the
  outcome.
  - **Related:** `errorText(TypeError)` shows "Something went wrong" instead of
  the network message. Wrapping the read loop's error in `ApiError(…, 0)` fixes
  both.

  **6. web/src/views/ReviewView.vue:44-58 — the whole review page is replaced by
  an error when only the estimate fails.**
  - **Defect:** an estimate failure sets `loadError`, which hides a campaign
  that loaded fine.
  - **Fix:** add `.catch(() => null)` to the estimate call. `counts` already
  falls back to `campaign.counts`.

  **7. Tests that don't prove what their names claim:**
  - web/src/campaign/composer.test.ts:13 — "even when its operator changes" uses
  the same operator (`within` → `within`). An operator change is never tested.
  - web/src/content/schedule.test.ts:34 — the UTC round-trip runs in whatever TZ
  the runner has. In Docker or CI with TZ=UTC it is an identity check and
  proves no conversion. Pin `process.env.TZ` (for example `Europe/Istanbul`) in
  the Vitest config or test setup.

  ### Checked and found sound
  - **Open redirect:** `safeRedirect` rejects `//` and `/\`. Redirects only go
  through vue-router, whose web history prefixes the page's own origin, so a
  cross-origin jump isn't possible.
  - **XSS:** there is no `v-html` or `innerHTML`. AI output, briefs, customer
  data, unsupported-brief reasons and server error details are all rendered as
  escaped text.
  - **401 handling:** 401s from the session endpoints are excluded. Elsewhere a
  401 clears the session and goes to sign-in with a redirect back; ContentView
  doesn't loop on a 401.
  - **Autosave queue:** the saver runs one save at a time and reads the version
  and payload when each save runs. Rule edits are built from the latest rules. A
  409 locks the page with a reload banner.
  - **Content tied to its campaign:** the RouterView is keyed by path, `id` is
  fixed per page instance, and the leave and update guards save before switching
  campaigns.
  - **Generation:** it asks before overwriting saved or typed text. It refetches
  after the stream and refuses to adopt a version someone else saved. Stop
  aborts the fetch, and leaving or unmounting also aborts it.
  - **Approval:** it needs an explicit when-choice, a "reviewed" checkbox and a
  confirm dialog that shows the time with its zone. Approval is sent with the
  version that was loaded, so stale content gets a 409. The schedule is
  re-checked against a ticking clock on every click. `datetime-local` is parsed
  as local time and sent as `toISOString()` (UTC). A suggestion is preselected
  only while it is still valid, which fits D29.
  - **Channels:** removing a channel that has content asks first (D38).
  - **Listeners and timers:** `beforeunload`, the review clock interval and the
  typing-pause timer are all cleaned up on unmount.
  - **Dialogs:** Reka AlertDialog and Dialog have titles and descriptions and
  handle focus and Escape. Form fields are labelled, errors are linked with
  `aria-describedby`, and the focused blocker list is announced.
  - **i18n:** `tr` is typed `Record<Key, …>`, so every key exists in both
  languages. I found no hard-coded English in the reviewed templates. Server and
  AI text is shown as untranslated details, as D44 intends.

  **Not checked:** DeliveryStatus, RecipientsDrawer, ResendDialog and the
  dashboard/list views (out of scope), and the Go handlers beyond content.go.

› Message from general-purpose
  ## Review of PR #6: monitoring and delivery frontend

  I found no critical defects. The numbers, cancel and resend targeting, URL
  handling and privacy all hold up. The one real gap is the live stream: when it
  closes for good, the page never finds out. The fixes are small and I made no
  edits.

  ### High
  None.

  ### Medium
  **1. A stream that closes for good shows "reconnecting…" forever.**
  `web/src/delivery/stream.ts:27` and
  `web/src/components/DeliveryStatus.vue:115,173`
  - `onerror` always calls `onTrouble(true)`. When the server answers a
  reconnect with a non-200 status (401 after the session expires, 404, a 500
  from `serverError` in `events.go:99`, or a 5xx from the dev proxy), the
  browser closes `EventSource` for good and never retries.
  - **Scenario:** the session expires during a send. The page keeps the "Live"
  pill and frozen counts, and the banner falsely says it is reconnecting.
  `onUnauthorized` never fires, so there is no redirect to sign in.
  - If the very first connect fails, the page sits on "Loading the delivery
  status…" forever, because the reconnecting alert only renders inside the
  `summary` branch. The scheduled phase never shows the alert either.
  - **Fix:**
    - In `onerror`, when `es.readyState === EventSource.CLOSED`, report a
  terminal state.
    - Make one `api('/api/me')` call so a 401 goes through `responseError`,
  which triggers sign-in.
    - Show a "stopped — retry" alert with a button that calls `connect()`.
    - Move the alert above the phase branches.
    - Add a `stream.test.ts` case for a closed source.

  **2. Cancelling while paused leaves the page showing the old send state.**
  `DeliveryStatus.vue:63`
  - `cancel()` reconnects only when not paused. The parent's campaign becomes
  `cancelled` (the status badge updates), but `snap` still says `sending`.
  - **Scenario:** the "Live" pill, the Pause button and "Cancel campaign…" all
  stay. A second cancel attempt fails with an error, and the counts never show
  the cancelled group.
  - **Fix:** set `paused.value = false` and always call `connect()` after a
  cancel.

  ### Low
  **3. "Live" pill shows while paused.** `DeliveryStatus.vue:68,164`: `live`
  ignores `paused`, so a paused page with a closed stream still says "Live".
  Fix: `&& !paused.value`.

  **4. Drawer can show the previous filter's rows.**
  `RecipientsDrawer.vue:37-65`
  - Closing sets `data = null` but does not bump `seq`. A request still in
  flight then refills `data`, and on reopen the new tab briefly shows the old
  tab's rows and reason box.
  - Switching tabs has the same brief mix: old rows and reasons under the newly
  selected tab and its info title.
  - Fix: `seq++` when `q` is null, and clear `data` when the group or channel
  changes.

  **5. Typing can be undone by a late URL update** (plausible).
  `RecipientsDrawer.vue:58`: after the 300 ms debounce, `router.replace`
  resolves asynchronously (it awaits `loadSession`). A key typed in that window
  is overwritten when the watcher sees `q.q !== search`. Confirm by typing
  during the replace with a slow guard. Fix: skip the sync while
  `document.activeElement` is the search input.

  **6. Back during a pending search adds a stray `?q=` to the URL.**
  `RecipientsDrawer.vue:76`: Back does not call `close()`, so the debounce timer
  survives. `set()` then runs with `query.value === null` and replaces the URL
  with `?q=…`. Fix: `clearTimeout` in the watcher when `q` is null, and guard
  `set()`.

  **7. Out-of-range pages.** `recipients.ts:46`
  - No upper bound is checked. `?page=1001` returns a 422 error with no pager,
  so the only way out is a tab change.
  - A page past the end offers only Prev, one page at a time.
  - Fix: clamp to 1000, and make Prev jump to `ceil(total/page_size)` when no
  rows come back.

  **8. Summary links open a narrower tab than the count they show.**
  `DeliveryStatus.vue:206,209`
  - "Not sent" opens the `failed` tab, which can be 0 while skipped is large.
  - "In progress" (pending + retrying) opens `pending` only.
  - Fix: open the first non-zero member group.

  **9. i18n and accessibility text.**
  - `RecipientsDrawer.vue:242`: `toLocaleLowerCase()` with no locale turns
  "İptal edildi" into "i̇ptal…" in a non-Turkish browser. Pass the current
  locale, or skip lowercasing for Turkish (that text already quotes the group).
  - `recipients.meta` is not pluralised ("1 messages"), and its sr-only
  description at line 146 renders "counts as of  (".
  - `delivery.rate.*` shows "rate-limited 0 requests… They retry automatically"
  on finished campaigns. Hide it when the count is 0.
  - `DeliveryStatus.vue:228`: the bar's `aria-label` leaves out `cancelled` and
  uses unformatted numbers, so for cancelled campaigns the spoken numbers don't
  add up.

  **10. Dashboard status counts come from the newest 200 campaigns only.**
  `DashboardView.vue:20`: there is no "newest 200" note like the campaigns page
  has. D49 mentions the cap only for the list. Fix: show the same
  `campaigns.limit` note when `list.length === 200`.

  ### Tests
  - `status.test.ts`, `recipients.test.ts` and `list.test.ts` do assert real
  behaviour: groups add up, estimate vs actual, every resend-offer state, URL
  round-trips and paging past the end.
  - `stream.test.ts` has no case for a terminal error (finding 1).
  - The component behaviour (pause, cancel reconnect, unmount close, the
  drawer's request-order guard) has no Vitest coverage and is covered only by
  the e2e scripts.

  ### Checked and sound
  - **Numbers:**
    - The seven groups add up to the audience.
    - Finished, sent and processed percentages divide by the right totals.
    - The estimate stays separate from the actual: people at approval vs
  messages per channel, labelled.
    - The difference compares messages to messages.
  - **Stream lifecycle:**
    - The previous stream is closed before reconnecting, and the stream is
  closed on `end` and on unmount.
    - Changing the campaign remounts the page, since `RouterView` is keyed by
  path.
    - No updates arrive after close.
  - **Cancel and resend:**
    - Cancel and resend use the right campaign id and channel.
    - Duplicate resends are blocked by `busy` and, server-side, by the unique
  index (409), with a refresh after a failure.
    - The stale offer after `end` (D36) is handled by navigating to the new
  draft.
  - **Drawer:**

    - Opening from a link replaces history instead of going back.

  there is a browser check for this).

  - **Privacy:**

⏺ Agent "Review PR #6 monitoring frontend" finished · 5m 0s

› Message from general-purpose
  ## Backend review of PR #6 (`origin/main...origin/milestone-f-frontend`,
  `internal/` and `cmd/`)

  I found no critical or high defects. Each finding below was checked by reading
  the code paths involved. I did not run tests, `go vet` or `go build`, because
  no Go toolchain is installed.

  ### Medium

  **1. Tests never exercise the new shortcut in the retries and 429 query**
  (`internal/campaign/events.go:211-215`)
  - **Defect:** The query skips messages where `status='sent' AND
  attempt_count=1`. Every events test fixture inserts messages with the default
  `attempt_count = 0`, so every message passes the filter and the skip is never
  tested. The e2e suite, which runs the real worker, never asserts `retries` or
  `rate_limited`.
  - **Failure scenario:** Someone changes the condition to `attempt_count <= 2`,
  or a future worker change records a 429 under a single claim. The dashboard
  then undercounts retries and 429s, and all tests still pass.
  - **I checked the reasoning behind the shortcut and it holds today:**
    - `Claim` (`queue.go:121`) is the only writer of `attempt_count`.
    - Every attempt row, including one recorded late after its lease was lost,
  comes from a claim.
    - So a message that is sent after one claim has exactly one attempt, the
  accepted one.
  - **Fix:** In `TestEvents_SnapshotCounts`, set `attempt_count` to match the
  seeded attempts. Add two cases and assert `retries` and `rate_limited` for
  both:
    - a sent message with `attempt_count=1` and one accepted attempt;
    - a sent message with `attempt_count=2` and attempts rate_limited →
  accepted.

  ### Low

  **2. `rate_limited_recent` stays frozen after the stream ends**
  (`events.go:120-126` with `:213`)
  - **Defect:** The last snapshot before `end` keeps its time-dependent "429s in
  the last 5 minutes" count, and then the stream closes (D36).
  - **Failure scenario:** A campaign finishes 1 minute after a burst of 40 429s.
  An open dashboard shows "40 rate-limited in the last 5 min" until it is
  reloaded, and a reload shows 0.
  - **Fix:** Set `RateLimitedRecent = 0` when the status is completed or
  cancelled and `!inFlight`, or have the UI hide it for finished campaigns.
  Whether users see this depends on the frontend, which I did not review.

  **3. Wrong reason for a message handed back unsent** (`events.go:125`,
  `reasonSQL` "retrying" → `coalesce(la.outcome,'requeued')`)
  - **Defect:** A message handed back on shutdown (`dispatch.go:231`, no attempt
  recorded) after an earlier attempt shows that earlier attempt's outcome
  instead of `requeued`.
  - **Failure scenario:** A message gets a 429, then on its next claim the
  worker shuts down while waiting for a send slot. Retrying shows
  `rate_limited`, although nothing was sent the second time.
  - **Fix:** This is cosmetic. Either accept it and note it in D46, or compare
  `la.attempt_no` with `m.attempt_count`.
  - **Related, but older than this PR:** `retries` counts `attempt_no > 1`, and
  `attempt_no` is the claim number. A hand-back followed by a success therefore
  counts as a retry with only one request sent.

  **4. Uncertain reason does not match D46's wording** (`events.go:114-115,
  124`)
  - **Defect:** D46 says uncertain is explained "by the last attempt's outcome".
  The code uses the latest attempt that got no clear answer (`lu`).
  - **Failure scenario:** Attempts timeout → rejected give the reason `timeout`.
  The test expects `timeout`, so the choice looks intended, but the decision
  record says otherwise.
  - **Fix:** Reword D46, which is better than changing the code.

  **5. A wrong `WEB_DIR` fails silently** (`cmd/scc/main.go:101`,
  `internal/spa/spa.go:892`)
  - **Defect:** Nothing checks at startup that `WEB_DIR/index.html` exists.
  - **Failure scenario:** With a wrong `WEB_DIR`, every page URL answers 404
  while the startup log reports a normal start.
  - **Fix:** `os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, "index.html"))` at startup, and refuse
  to start if it fails.

  ### Checked and found sound
  - **Auth:** every new route (`/api/catalog`, `DELETE`, `/channels`,
  `/request`, `/recipients`) is registered on the `api` mux, which
  `auth.Require` wraps. The SPA at `/` does not shadow `/api/`, and it only
  answers GET and HEAD.
  - **SQL:**
    - Every user value is passed as a parameter, including the name search.
    - `fold()` substitutes only fixed text, and LIMIT/OFFSET come from validated
  integers.
    - The LIKE escaping (`\ % _`) matches Postgres's default escape character,
  and a test covers it.
  - **Privacy:** contacts are masked on the server and the mask is safe for
  non-ASCII text. The `error` and `last_error` columns are never selected, the
  city is used only to compute the over-limit detail, and `Cache-Control:
  no-store` is set. Page is limited to 1–1000, the search to 50 characters, and
  group and channel are allow-listed.
  - **Locking and transactions:**
    - `deleteDraft` does `FOR UPDATE` plus a guarded delete, and a concurrent
  test covers approve against delete.
    - `updateChannels` updates under the version check and deletes the content
  in the same transaction. A concurrent content save fails as stale because the
  version was bumped.
    - `updateRequest` checks the version before the AI call and again when
  saving, and validates the text through `Interpret`.
    - No other table references a draft, so deleting one cannot break a foreign
  key.
  - **Groups:** `groupSQL` puts every status in exactly one of the seven groups,
  so they add up to the audience. The snapshot and the recipients counts come
  from one repeatable-read, read-only transaction. A test checks that groups add
  up to the audience.
  - **Resources:** every `Query` goes through `ForEachRow` or `CollectRows`,
  which close the rows, and the transactions are rolled back on defer. The
  `windowCap.waiting` test hook is nil in production.
  - **Performance at ~6,000 messages:** lookups go through
  `messages_campaign_status_idx` and the `UNIQUE(message_id, attempt_no)` index.
  The per-attempt lookups run only for the reason counts and the 50 rows of a
  page.
  - **Migrations:** 00004 then 00005 adds and drops the `name` column, both roll
  back cleanly, and no code still uses `name`.
  - **Catalog:** `Fields` and `Limits` hand out copies, and a test checks every
  declared value type against `Validate`.

  Not checked: the frontend's use of these fields, and CSRF for the new PUT and
  DELETE routes. The auth model is unchanged by this PR.

  Where the time went

  ┌───────────────────┬─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
  │       Step        │  Approximate    │                Why                │
  │                   │      time       │                                   │

  │ Single-file       │ about 1–2 min   │ Each run reinstalls Playwright's  │
  │ browser runs      │ each, many      │ packages and starts a fresh       │
  │ while fixing      │ times           │ browser.                          │
  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │                   │ one lost make   │ I chained it behind a git command │
  │ My mistakes       │ test run        │  that failed, so it never started │
  │                   │                 │  and I had to rerun it later.     │
  └───────────────────┴─────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

  The same Go tests got 5–6× slower during the day. Early on, internal/campaign
  took 20 s, internal/db 26 s and internal/worker 20 s. In the final run they
  took 140 s, 156 s and 96 s. The tests didn't grow that much. The cause is
  contention: Docker has 8 CPUs and 8 GB shared by the running app stack, the
  test database, the Go build and the browser. On top of that, Go tests up to 8
  packages at once against one Postgres.

  The bottlenecks

  1. Every Go test builds its own database from scratch. internal/campaign alone
     has 67 places that create a fresh database, and each one runs all
     migrations. Seven tests also generate the full 3,000-customer seed.
  2. make test runs Go and the frontend one after the other, and the frontend
     part always reinstalls its packages before the type check and Vitest.
  3. Browser checks wait for real sends to finish. One send goes to about 2,100
     SMS customers at 100/s, about 21 s. The mock provider fails about 9% of
     requests on purpose (errors, 429s and timeouts), and those messages retry
     with backoff of up to 30 s per attempt. So "wait until completed" can take
     minutes. Five browser files each start their own sends.
  4. The browser suite reinstalls Playwright's packages on every run, and
     testing a frontend change needs a full image rebuild.
  5. Everything shares one Docker machine, so running more in parallel without
     fixing the above makes each part slower.
  6. My own process:
     - I ran the race detector on everything instead of only the changed
       packages.
     - I reran full suites after small fixes.
     - The broken command chain cost one extra run.

  How to speed it up without losing coverage

  Ranked by the time they save:

  #: 1
  Change: Template databases: run migrations once into a template database, and
  create each test's database as a copy (CREATE DATABASE … TEMPLATE). Same for
  a seeded template for the tests that need 3,000 customers.
  Expected effect: Go suite likely 2–4× faster; the seed tests most
  Coverage: Same tests, same isolation
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 2
  Change: Throwaway Postgres settings for the test database: turn off fsync,
  synchronous_commit and full_page_writes. It's already on tmpfs, and the data
  is discarded anyway.
  Expected effect: Fewer disk waits, especially with many tests at once
  Coverage: Unchanged; production settings are separate
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 3
  Change: Run Go and the frontend at the same time in make test.
  Expected effect: Wall time becomes the longer of the two, not their sum (about

  1 min saved)
  Coverage: Unchanged
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 4
  Change: Skip reinstalling packages when the lockfile hasn't changed, for both
  the frontend tests and the browser suite.
  Expected effect: About 20–40 s saved per run
  Coverage: Unchanged
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 5
  Change: A separate, faster stack for the browser suite: its own Compose
  project
  with a throwaway database, shorter mock-provider delays and a configurable
  backoff cap (for example 2 s instead of 30 s).
  Expected effect: The minutes-long waits for retries become seconds. It also
  stops filling your local data with test campaigns
  Coverage: The same code paths and failures. Only the waiting times are
  shorter,
  and the real 30 s cap stays covered by the backend tests
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 6
  Change: Share sends between browser files: send the long-SMS campaign and the
  large campaign once per run and reuse them in recipients, resend, live and
  review-fixes.
  Expected effect: Roughly half as many sends
  Coverage: Every check stays. The files just share the setup
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 7
  Change: Run independent browser files in parallel. The dashboard-count file
  has
  to stay alone, because other files' sends would change its numbers.
  Expected effect: Shorter full run, once #5 removes the long waits
  Coverage: Unchanged
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 8
  Change: The race detector on changed packages during work, and on everything
  once before merging.
  Expected effect: Saves about 5 min per loop
  Coverage: The full race run still happens before every merge
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 9
  Change: My process: focused tests while fixing, full suites once at the end,
  long runs in the background while I write docs, and no slow command chained
  behind a fragile one.
  Expected effect: The biggest saving in practice
  Coverage: Unchanged

  What I would not do: drop the real sends, lower the mock provider's failure
  rates, or skip the race detector entirely. Those find the problems that
  matter.

  All of this is measured from this session's logs. I haven't benchmarked the
  fixes themselves, so the gains are estimates. Items 1–5 and 8 fit the T19
  plan's performance and delivery phases. Should I add them there, and measure
  before and after so the speedups are real numbers?

⏺ I mostly agree with the order: quality first, then the extra features, then
  documentation and delivery. I'd change five things, because as written the
  split has two gaps and a few ordering problems.

  What I'd change

  1. Add a security review to T19. It's in neither your T19 nor T21, and it
  matters more for delivery than any bonus feature:
  - No login brute-force limit. Nothing limits failed sign-ins today.
  - Only one security header. The app sends frame-ancestors and nothing else: no
    full CSP, nosniff or Referrer-Policy on the app.
  - A pushed session export contains your real email. It's in ai-sessions/04,
    which is already on GitHub, and CASE §8 requires the exports to be checked
    for personal information. This should be handled at the start of T19, not in
    T21: every new export adds to the problem, and removing it from Git history
    is a decision you need to make.

  2. Move CI from T20 to T19, right after the test speed-ups. CI isn't really a
  bonus: it guards every change in T20 and T21, and it's cheap because make test
  already runs in Docker. It also depends on the test work. Today's final run
  showed two timing-sensitive tests failing under load, so harden and speed up
  the tests first, then turn CI on. The browser suite could run in CI later,
  nightly or on request, because it needs the full stack and takes minutes.

  3. Move the final UI/UX audit from T19 to T21. T20 adds screens: language
  variants and A/B variants in the composer, review and delivery. An audit at
  the end of T19 would miss them, so it should run once on the finished product,
  just before delivery. T19 keeps its exploratory QA.

  4. Start OpenAPI in T19, not T21. T19 changes the campaigns API, and T20
  changes content, approval and delivery for languages and variants. If the spec
  and its drift test (the test that fails when routes and spec disagree) exist
  before those changes, each change updates the spec as it's made and the test
  enforces it. T21 then adds Swagger UI and polish rather than documenting a
  moving API afterwards.

  5. Rethink T20's size and order. Both features change the core send path, and
  together they multiply it.
  - Recipient language is CASE's optional feature, and the data half-exists:
    2,672 users are tr and 328 en, but nobody is de, and the worker and content
    code ignore language today. It affects:
    - generation (the AI writes 2–3 versions), the editors, previews and
      character limits per version;
    - the over-limit estimate, the approval check, the worker's choice of
      version, resend, and recipient details;
    - the seed (D28), to add German speakers.
  - A/B variants multiply that again: variants × languages × channels. I'd also
    question its value as specified. The mock providers only report "accepted",
    so without opens, clicks or conversions there is no outcome to compare. A/B
    would be a split with nothing to judge it by, unless we also simulate an
    outcome, which is more scope.
  - My recommendation: do language first, fully, with one content model designed
    upfront so variants can be added later without rework. Then do A/B only if
    time allows, with an agreed success metric. If time is short, drop A/B
    rather than cut quality.

  Agreements and smaller notes

  - Server-side pagination, search and filtering: a good call, but it replaces
    D49, which we decided on, so it gets a new decision. It must include
    server-side status counts: the dashboard cards currently count only the
    newest 200 campaigns, which becomes wrong at scale. Keep it small: status
    filter, brief search (Turkish-folded, the same approach as the recipient
    search), paging and counts.
  - Sidebar scrolling, logout accessibility, responsive layouts: agreed. The QA
    screenshots already showed one example: the sidebar's mode badge wraps in
    Turkish.
  - Test speed-ups: template databases, throwaway Postgres settings, Go and
    frontend in parallel, cached installs, and a faster dedicated stack for the
    browser suite. That stack would also stop test campaigns piling up in your
    local data.
  - A light performance check should stay in T19: a full 6,000-message send and
    several live screens at once. Your split dropped it, and it's cheap.
  - "Keep Mock/Real AI and document the key setup": most of it exists already.
    It's a T21 documentation item, not T20 work.
  - "Product Analysis and Roadmap": fine for T21 and not required by CASE.md, so
    keep it short.
  - T21's fresh-clone check: essential. CASE §8 is judged on docker compose up
    from a clean clone.

  Remaining gaps

  1. "Data isolation" needs a definition. Today every marketer sees every
  campaign and its recipients by design (D10, a single role). There are two
  possible meanings:
  - Keep D10: isolation means protecting customer data around the app. Masked
    contacts, no customer data sent to Claude (D15), the mock provider's
    restricted database role (D6), no personal data in logs or errors, and API
    checks on every route.
  - Per-marketer ownership: each marketer sees only their own campaigns. That
    changes a business decision, and touches every query, the dashboard counts
    and the tests.

  This is the one question below.

  2. The pre-commit scan should be a tool, not just my habit. I'd add a
  repeatable scan, for example make scan using a pinned secret scanner
  (gitleaks) run in Docker. It runs before each commit, and in CI on every push,
  so the rule doesn't depend on me remembering. It would be the first item of
  T19. The scanner is new tooling, so it needs your OK, though it's not an app
  dependency.

  3. The session exports fall under the rule. 05, 06 and the upcoming 07 contain
  your email and name in the text. Under the new rule they're redacted before
  they're committed, as part of each milestone's wrap-up. 04, already pushed,
  stays as you decided.

  4. Performance testing needs targets. Otherwise "done" isn't measurable. I'd
  propose numbers at the start of T19 for you to approve, for example:
  - a 6,000-message send finishes within about 1.5× the theoretical time at
    100/s;
  - API reads stay under 200 ms at 10 concurrent marketers;
  - 20 open live screens use less than one CPU core of database time.

  5. OpenAPI in T21 means the spec is written after the API stops changing.
  That's fine if T21 includes the drift test, so the spec can't silently diverge
  later. I'll write it then.

  6. T20 starts with decisions, not code:
  - One content model that supports languages now and variants later.
  - The fallback rule. I'd propose English is required for every campaign, so
    every recipient always gets a message.
  - German speakers in the seed, for new installs only (D28).
  - Per-language length rules. Turkish and German characters force the shorter
    SMS encoding (70 characters per segment instead of 160), though the
    160-character limit stays.
  - Real-AI cost: writing 3 languages triples the generated text per campaign.
  - The A/B evaluation's output is a decision record with a recommendation. It's
    built only if you approve it.

  7. Small items to fold into T19's QA:
  - the two low findings left from the PR review (the retry count after a
    hand-back, and the connection-drop race);
  - the Turkish sidebar wrap;

    solves.

          +heir default failure rates. "p95" is the 95th percentile over

          +s): 95% final within **45 s**, all final within **90 s** of se
          +nding starting. The theoretical minimum is 30 s at 100/s per c
          +hannel; the rest is retries (1, 2, 4, 8 s) and 5 s timeouts. |
          + Start and finish times from the database |

          +s included. A hard requirement, not a target. | Sliding window

          +gn, estimate, recipients, edits): p95 **≤ 200 ms** for reads a

          +rors. | `make perf` load test |

  What I built
  - make scan checks every file Git tracks or would add, so a local .env or
    node_modules is never read, plus the commits not pushed yet. It uses
    gitleaks from a pinned Docker image (v8.24.3); nothing is installed.
  - make hooks installs a pre-commit hook that scans the staged changes. It's
    enabled in this clone.
  - make scan-selftest plants secrets in a throwaway repository and requires
    each to be caught by its own rule:

  | Planted                      | Caught                   |
  |------------------------------|--------------------------|
  | Anthropic key                | ✓                        |
  | GitHub token                 | ✓                        |
  | 2 email addresses            | ✓                        |
  | 3 phone numbers              | ✓                        |
  | .env file                    | ✓                        |
  | the project's fictional data | not flagged, as intended |

  - .gitleaks.toml adds the project's own rules to gitleaks' built-in ones. It
    allows only fictional seed and test data, placeholders, the demo login and
    masked contacts.
  - README: a new "Scanning for secrets and personal data" section.

  Problems found and fixed along the way
  1. gitleaks v8.24.3 doesn't recognize Anthropic keys, the very key this
     project uses. The self-test exposed it, so the project config adds a rule
     for them.
  2. The pre-commit hook let one planted key through once. I undid that commit
     immediately, with nothing pushed. I couldn't reproduce it in 3 more tries.
     The likely cause is Docker on macOS reading .git a moment out of date right
     after git add. The staged scan now copies the staged files on this machine
     and streams them into the container, so it no longer depends on that.
     After the change, all 5 test commits with a planted key were blocked, a
     force-added .env was blocked, and a harmless change passed.
  3. Two test fixtures were flagged.
     - The sign-in test's Marketer@Example.COM: the allowance for example.com is
       now case-insensitive.
     - The masking test's +4915112345678: it could be a real German mobile
       number, so it's replaced by a UK number reserved for fiction.

  the send time, so slow machines get a clear diagnostic instead of a
  misleading failure.

  Coverage is the same or better. All 341 baseline Go tests still run and pass
  (checked by name), plus 4 new ones. Statement coverage went from 81.5% to 
  82.1%, Vitest still has 333 tests, and the browser suite still has 181 checks.

  A fair old-versus-new comparison, alternating both versions under the same
  conditions, gave 111 s against 90 s before the last two changes. Single
  timings on this laptop vary a lot: the same run took between 75 and 112 s in
  one series.

  What made the difference (each measured)

  1. A template database: each Go test copies one migrated database instead of
     migrating its own, cutting campaign from 71 to 35 s.
  2. Parallel tests in the db and e2e packages, which were the slowest.
  3. Go and frontend tests run at the same time, and frontend packages are
     reinstalled only when the lockfile changes.
  4. go vet runs only in make lint, no longer duplicated in make test. And
     TestEndToEnd uses a 2 s retry cap; its retries still happen.
  5. The browser suite on its own stack (D53), in two lanes with one shared
     send. It no longer touches your local app or its data, and nothing needs to
     be running first.

  Planned but not kept, with the evidence

  - Turning off Postgres durability settings: no measurable gain, because the
    test database is already in memory.
  - Shorter mock-provider delays: no possible gain, because sending is limited
    by the 100/s rate, not the provider's response time.
  - Faster health checks on the browser-suite stack: no measurable gain, so I
    reverted it.
  - A seeded template database: seeding happens in only a few tests that aren't
    on the slowest path, so it wasn't worth adding.

  Flaky tests found and fixed

  1. The provider role's password being changed by two packages at once ("tuple
     concurrently updated"). This also failed on main during the comparison.
     It's now serialized, with a regression test that failed every time before
     the fix.
  2. A worker test whose 400 ms window could expire during setup. It's now 3 s,
     and fails with a clear message if the worker never waited.
  3. A provider test that slept 400 ms instead of waiting for the stored result.
  4. The scheduled-send check: it now has a 2 s margin, and the database's clock
     confirms the check ran before the send time.

  Commits

  1. 451ca20 feat: RETRY_BACKOFF_MAX can lower the retry cap. Default 30 s,
     lower only; Retry-After still wins.
  2. 8d611c4 test: template databases, parallel db and e2e tests, no timing
     guesses.
  3. a6b138e build: Go and frontend together; the browser suite on its own
     stack.
  4. 51ad438 docs: the measurements in docs/performance.md, the README test
     section, and a D53 history note.

  Lint is clean. Each commit passed the pre-commit scan, and a final make scan
  over the 8 unpushed commits was clean too.

  Things to know:
  - Laptop variance is real. The first runs after a rebuild or other activity
    take up to 83 s (make test) and 139 s (make e2e).
  - Stack startup isn't included in the browser target. About 25 s of each make 
    e2e goes to starting and removing its stack; I counted the suite itself
    against the target.
  - One TDD lapse. I wrote the backoff and setting tests first, but first ran
    them after implementing.
  - Cleanup: I removed my temporary comparison checkout. Its Docker volumes
    (project sccbase, build caches only) are still on disk. I can remove them if
    you want.

⏺ Understood: the final CI strategy, then step 4, and PR #7 stays unmerged.
  First, the design that avoids redundant runs.

  Where duplicates would come from. Every commit pushed to a branch with an open
  PR fires two events, push and pull_request. Running both would test the same
  code twice. The two runs aren't identical, though: the PR run tests the commit
  merged with main, which catches integration problems. So for a branch with an
  open PR, the PR run should be the one that runs.

  CI (test, lint, scan):
  - Every push runs it, except pushes to a branch that has an open PR. A small
    first job checks for an open PR and skips the rest.
  - Every PR runs it through the PR event.
  - Pushes to main always run it.

  Browser checks: every PR, every push to main, nightly, and on request. The
  temporary path-based trigger goes, since PRs now cover it.

  Stale runs: a new commit cancels the same PR's or branch's older run.

  The final CI strategy, verified on GitHub

  ┌──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │  What runs   │               When                │       Verified       │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │ test, lint,  │ every push and every PR           │ ✅                   │
  │ scan         │                                   │                      │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │ Browser      │ every PR, every push to main,     │ ✅ PR runs: 181 of   │
  │ checks       │ nightly, and on request           │ 181 checks           │
  └──────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

  No commit is tested twice. A push to a branch with an open PR is left to the
  PR's run, which tests the commit merged with main. On this PR's pushes, the
  push run's gate skipped all three jobs, and a newer commit cancels the older
  run. D52 and the README describe the strategy.

  The nightly schedule and the "Run workflow" button only become active once the
  workflow is on main.

  Step 4: findings and results (details in docs/security-review.md)

  Automated checks:
  - govulncheck: 0 vulnerabilities in code the app uses. It lists one advisory
    in an unused part of golang.org/x/crypto (openpgp), for which no fix exists.
  - npm audit: 0 vulnerabilities.
  - The scan: clean.

  Already sound, with evidence:
  - Customer data:
    - contacts are masked by the server;
    - the live status stream carries only counts;
    - the AI never receives customer data, by construction;
    - logs hold no personal data;
    - the provider's database role is limited to its own table.
  - Sessions: random tokens stored only as hashes, a fresh token at each
    sign-in, HttpOnly and SameSite cookies, a fixed lifetime.
  - SQL: no query is built from user input. I traced every variable SQL fragment
    to constants or numbered parameters.
  - No XSS openings: nothing is inserted as raw HTML.
  - The rest: request size limits, generic error messages, and a non-root
    container.

  Fixed, each with a failing test first:
  1. Failed sign-ins are now limited (D55): 5 per 15 minutes per email and per
     address, then a 429 checked before the password. The sign-in page explains
     it in English and Turkish.
  2. Requests from other sites are refused when they try to change something or
     sign in. This adds a second layer behind SameSite=Lax.
  3. Customer data is never cached by the browser: every API response is
     no-store, nosniff and no-referrer.
  4. A strict Content Security Policy: no inline scripts or styles, no framing
     by other sites. The browser suite now fails on any violation. I proved the
     detector works with a planted violation, and the full suite ran clean,
     locally and in CI.
  5. The session cookie is now Secure whenever the request comes over HTTPS.
  6. Idle connections now close after 2 minutes.
  7. A new test checks that every API route requires a session. It reads the
     routes from the source, so future routes are covered automatically.

  Decided against, with the reason:
  - A read timeout on the server: Go's version would also cut the live status
    stream and the AI-writing stream. Bodies are size-capped instead.
  - A test that captures log output: the worker only logs on database errors, so
    the test would have passed trivially. I reviewed every log call instead.
  - A browser check for the sign-in lockout: all browser files sign in from the
    same address, so a lockout test would block the files running alongside it.

  Remaining risks (documented)

  - The sign-in limit is kept in memory per api process: it resets on a restart,
    and behind a proxy all clients share one address.
  - AI calls have no rate limit: a cost risk in real mode, not a data risk.
  - Expired sessions stay in the database. They can't be used, but nothing
    cleans them up.

    - search follows typing after a short pause;

    - a late server answer can't overwrite a newer one;

  Main findings
  - Nothing is compressed when served. Every first visit downloads 263–294 kB of
    JavaScript instead of about 95 kB. On the phone profile the sign-in page
    first appears after about 4.6 s, and almost all of that is download and
    round trips. This matters far more than the chunk size, so I added it to the
    README's known limitations.
  - The 43.9 kB chunk doesn't need more work. On the phone profile, compiling
    and running all the JavaScript takes about 350 ms, and this chunk accounts
    for at most about 150 ms of it. Splitting it would not reduce what is
    downloaded, and Vue's runtime alone is about 43 kB.
  - Phone interactions are slow in two places. Redrawing the list after a status
    filter takes 400–480 ms, and switching back to English takes 336–432 ms. On
    desktop every interaction takes 64 ms or less.
  - P3–P5 slow down because requests compete for CPU, not because of a bad 
    query. The heaviest statements take 10–12 ms on their own and about 40 ms
    when ten run at once.
  - Live screens each query on their own. Each open screen runs its own database
    queries every second, so the database cost grows with the number of
    screens.
  - Test durations vary for two reasons. A run takes as long as its slowest
    package, campaign: 32 s alone, 70–95 s in the full run, because its 82 tests
    run one after another. Host load does the rest: today it ranged from 5
    to 98. Browser and editor apps were busy, and your local app stack uses
    about 0.3 CPU even when idle. The test count barely grew (233 → 248 Go
    tests), so growth isn't the cause.

  Caveats
  - The machine wasn't quiet during these runs, and numbers move by about ±30%
    between runs.
  - The load generator runs in the same Docker VM as the stack it measures.
  - The phone figures come from a throttled desktop Chromium, not a real phone.

  Recommendations, each to be measured before and after
  1. Serve compressed assets. Compress the built files when the image is built
     and serve the compressed copy when the browser accepts it, using only the
     standard library. This is small, low-risk and has the biggest effect on
     loading.
  2. Share one poller per campaign for live screens (P6). One snapshot per
     second would serve all screens of a campaign, instead of one per screen.
     This was already listed as the upgrade path.
  3. Make the campaign, worker and other database packages run their tests in 
     parallel (T1). Each test already has its own database copy. I'd confirm it
     with 5 more runs to make sure nothing becomes flaky.
  4. Make filtering and the language switch faster on phones by redrawing less
     of the page when they happen.
  5. Settle how P3–P5 are read, either as realistic marketers (met) or back to
     back (missed). Meeting the back-to-back reading would need a migration (a
     stored last-attempt time and a search index), so I would not do it now.

⏺ I have changed no code. The proposals are recorded under Open Questions in
  DECISIONS.md, entries Q1–Q6. They aren't decisions yet, and the file is not
  committed.

  1. Live-status queries: agree, with a simpler alternative
  - Where I agree: stay in-process, and add no Redis or Kafka.
  - What I'd change: instead of one poller per campaign that pushes to
    subscribers, keep each stream's loop as it is and read the snapshot through
    a short-lived cache shared per campaign. When several streams ask at once,
    they wait for the same database read.
  - Why it's simpler: it gives the same saving with no start/stop logic for
    subscribers and no handling of slow subscribers. A shared poller is easy to
    get subtly wrong when the last viewer leaves just as a new one arrives.
  - Expected gain: database cost per campaign instead of per screen, about 1–2
    s/s down to roughly 0.1 s/s with 20 screens.
  - Trade-off: updates can be up to about 1.5 s old instead of about 1 s, which
    is still within the 2 s target.
  - Hidden risk: a database error must close every stream so browsers reconnect,
    and the cache must drop campaigns nobody is watching.

  2. Compressed assets: agree, with one refinement
  - Compress the files once when the image is built, rather than on every
    request. That costs no CPU per request and needs less code.
  - Expected gain: 263–294 kB down to about 95 kB per first visit. On slow 4G
    that is roughly a second off the first paint; on a local desktop connection
    the difference is small.
  - Risk: the response must keep the original content type, because the nosniff
    header blocks scripts with the wrong type. It also needs a Vary header. Both
    can be tested.
  - No Vue chunk splitting: agreed.

  3. Test audit: agree, but it's the wrong first move for speed
  - Step 7 showed the time is spent waiting, not on test count. campaign runs
    its 82 tests one after another: 32 s of wall time but only 9 s of CPU.
  - Cheaper, safer fix: run the database-backed packages' tests in parallel.
    Each test already has its own database copy. I estimate 76 s down to about
    55–65 s, and I'd confirm it with 5 consecutive runs.
  - The audit should still happen, but produce a list for you to approve item by
    item. Removing tests to save a few seconds would lose coverage for little
    gain.
  - The slow browser checks are slow because they really send campaigns at the
    rate limit. Moving checks from the browser to Go is worth considering per
    check, but it gains less than it seems.
  - Risk: tests that share process state, such as metrics and the sign-in
    throttle, must stay serial.

  4. Desktop first: agree
  - Keep the step 6 responsive checks; they're cheap.
  - Defer the phone-only slowness: the list redraw (400–480 ms) and the language
    switch.
  - Compression (item 2) helps phones anyway.

  5. Frontend issues: mostly already done
  - The fixed sidebar and a reachable Log out shipped in step 6, and
    e2e/responsive.mjs checks them.
  - Pagination is a real gap: on a 1440×900 screen, 25 rows push the pager below
    the fold. I'd add a compact pager above the list ("1–25 of 300", Previous,
    Next) and keep the one below. That's small, and both get browser checks.

  6. Transparency: agree
  - Targets stay unchanged.
  - P3–P5 are the one place where reading matters. The target doesn't say
    whether marketers pause between requests. With realistic pauses they're met;
    back to back, at about 14× that traffic, they're missed. I'd report both
    and let you choose which one counts as "met" (Q6).

  Proposed plan, in priority order

  Essential:
  1. Compressed assets (Q2). Small change; the biggest effect on loading.
  2. Shared snapshot cache for live screens (Q1). Fixes P6.
  3. Pager above the campaign list (Q5). Small.
  4. Parallel database tests (Q3, first half). Aimed at T1.

  Each is measured before and after with make perf or timed runs, run back to

  ## Browser and Vitest test audit (read-only: nothing edited, nothing run)

  Your per-file times show which savings actually shorten a run. The sending
  lane (delivery + recipients + resend + live + review-fixes) adds up to about
  63–80 s. The UI lane adds up to about 39–65 s. campaigns.mjs (3–5 s) runs
  alone before both. So only cuts in the sending lane or in campaigns.mjs make
  the whole run shorter. Cuts in the UI lane save CPU, but the run takes just as
  long.

  The three security risks

  1. Sign-in limits are kept in memory, per API process. Recommendation: keep as
  is, no change.
  - There is one API process, and a restart needs operator access.
  - The per-email limit protects each account even if the per-address limit is
    bypassed.
  - Each guess costs a bcrypt check.
  - Storing the limits in Postgres would need a migration and a database write
    on every failed sign-in. That only pays off with several API replicas.
  - One residual risk remains: anyone who knows an email address can lock that
    account out for 15 minutes (accepted in D55).
  - If the app is ever deployed behind a proxy, a trusted-proxy setting would be
    needed, because otherwise all clients would share the proxy's address.
    That's deferred until such a deployment.

  2. AI calls have no rate limit. Recommendation: fix (real mode only).
  - This is a cost risk, not a data risk: every create, brief edit and message
    generation can make up to two paid calls.
  - Proposed fix: a per-marketer limiter on those three routes, using the
    rate-limit library the sign-in throttle already uses. It answers 429 with a
    wait time and has its own UI message, because 429 currently shows the
    sign-in text.
  - It applies only when real AI is on. Mock AI is free, and the browser suite
    creates many drafts quickly.
  - The default would be configurable; I'd suggest about 60 calls per hour per
    marketer.
  - I'd also document setting a spend limit in the Anthropic console, which is
    the real cost ceiling.

  3. Expired sessions are never deleted. Recommendation: fix with one statement.
  - Expired sessions can't be used, because the expiry is checked, so the risk
    is only that the table keeps growing.
  - Fix: delete expired sessions when someone signs in. The expiry column is
    already indexed, and one test would cover it.
  - A scheduled cleanup job in the worker would also work, but it's more code
    for the same result.

  Security
  - AI call limit (D63):
    - With real AI, each marketer can make at most AI_CALLS_PER_HOUR provider
      calls (default 10) in any 60 minutes. You can change it in .env.
    - Every actual call counts, including the retry inside one brief
      interpretation or message generation.
    - Over the limit, the API answers 429 with a Retry-After header and the code
      ai_call_limit. Generating messages streams its result, so the limit is
      checked before streaming starts; a retry refused mid-stream ends with the
      same message.
    - The UI says how long to wait, in English and Turkish.
    - Mock AI is not limited.
    - Tests cover the sliding window, retries counting, the 429 before
      streaming, the refusal mid-stream, and the setting. With the limit
      disabled, the request tests fail, so they do test it.
  - Expired sessions: signing in now deletes them, with a test.
